anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to read, scan, or hold far more data and resources than the true business logic requires.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Internal buffer-manager hot pages and their associated latches become points of intense contention, stalling sessions on page access, pin, or flush operations.

When both conditions exist simultaneously, end-user statements display extreme and highly variable latency, slow-query logs fill with repetitive statements, CPU usage oscillates between long spin-loops and idle waits, and wait-event views show surges in buffer busy waits, page/latch waits, and I/O stalls. Hot root or leaf pages of frequently scanned tables and indexes become choke points, while oversized scans and long-lived transactions keep those pages in memory and pinned, amplifying contention. Application retries and lock time-outs rise, throughput collapses under concurrency, and even background tasks such as checkpoints or purge/clean-up jobs begin to lag.

Causal chain: inefficient SQL patterns (full-table scans, wide projections, chatty ORM loops, or monotonic inserts) read and dirty large numbers of pages, driving rapid buffer turnover and concentrating access on a small subset of pages. This inflates latch acquisition frequency and duration on those pages. The resulting latch waits extend statement and transaction lifetimes, which in turn leave pages pinned longer, exacerbate page hot-spotting, and further reduce effective cache capacity. The two anomalies thus reinforce each other in a feedback loop where poor workload logic produces the very contention that magnifies its own performance cost, degrading both transactional and analytical operations across the system.

entry.official_definition: Sets the interval between optional checks that the client is still connected while running queries.
entry.trigger_condition: During a long-running query, PostgreSQL polls the socket at this interval and can detect a closed connection sooner.
entry.workload_impact: Long-running queries can be aborted sooner after the kernel reports that the client connection is closed.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, disabling connection checks.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
